micro-immunity-disorders: What are the four categories of immunopathology?
Allergy, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency and cancer
Where are mast cells found, and what do they carry?
On epithelial surfaces, with surface IgE
Why do allergic reactions use the same machinery as antiparasitic defense?
Many allergens resemble parasitic antigens
How many people are heavily and persistently infected with helminths?
About one billion
What is familial about allergy?
A generalized predisposition
What antibody class mediates type I hypersensitivity?
IgE
What do the antibodies bind in type II hypersensitivity?
Cell surface antigens
What happens to the immune complexes in type III hypersensitivity?
They embed in basement membranes
What mediates type IV hypersensitivity?
T cells
What immunogenic forms do allergens take?
Proteins, and low molecular weight haptens
What happens on the sensitizing dose in type I allergy?
B cells form IgE, which arms mast cells
Which are the general targets of a type I reaction?
Skin, airway, gut and conjunctiva
What produces urticaria?
Mast cells in the skin releasing histamine
What happens in the nose during allergic rhinitis?
Histamine raises capillary permeability
Why does a food allergen produce urticaria in the skin?
Antigen enters blood vessels and is carried to the skin
What is the acute response in allergic asthma?
Bronchial smooth muscle contraction with increased mucus
What characterizes systemic anaphylaxis?
Sudden respiratory and circulatory disruption
How does epinephrine act in anaphylaxis?
It reforms tight junctions and relaxes bronchi
When does the late phase reaction occur?
About six hours afterwards
What does FEV1 measure?
Air forcibly exhaled in one second
Why does it matter to distinguish allergy from infection?
They present similarly but differ entirely
What are the three general methods of managing type I hypersensitivity?
Prevention, pharmacology, desensitization
What does prevention of allergy involve?
Modifying environment and behavior
How do corticosteroids act in allergy?
They inhibit lymphocytes to reduce IgE
What is the most common form of allergen specific immunotherapy?
Subcutaneous immunotherapy
Name two examples of type II hypersensitivity.
Transfusion reactions and Rh incompatibility
Why must ABO antigens be matched in transfusion?
There are no MHC molecules on red blood cells
What does the cross-match test compare?
Recipient serum against donor red cells
What are the consequences of a transfusion reaction?
Red cell destruction, glomerular blockage, fever and jaundice
When does an Rh negative person produce anti-Rh antibodies?
Only after sensitization
Which combination produces hemolytic disease of the newborn?
An Rh negative mother with an Rh positive fetus
When is Rhogam administered?
At 26 to 28 weeks, and after birth
What causes serum sickness?
Exposure to foreign animal proteins
How is allergy or hypersensitivity defined?
An exaggerated, misdirected immune response to an allergen
What do eosinophils release in an IgE response?
Toxic mediators
What immune response does helminth infection stimulate?
CD4 TH2-like responses with high IgE
micro-diagnosing-infections: Into which three categories do methods of identifying unknown microbes fall?
Phenotypic, genotypic and immunological
What does microscopic morphology examine?
Cell shape, size, stain reaction and cell structures
What is blood agar used to detect?
Hemolytic activity
What does the Kirby-Bauer disk-diffusion test give you?
Which drug is effective, and at what dose
What must be considered about any organism recovered from a specimen?
Whether it is causing disease or is normal flora
How should all specimens be regarded?
As potentially infectious
Which two routes can specimen analysis take?
Direct tests, or cultivation and isolation
Which stains are used for immediate direct examination?
Gram stain and acid-fast stain
What is the major practical advantage of genotypic methods?
Culture is not necessary
What instrument does the polymerase chain reaction use?
A thermal cycler
Which ribosomal RNA gene is used for prokaryotes?
What do immunological methods take advantage of?
Antigen-antibody specificity
What is serology?
In vitro diagnostic testing of serum samples
What does agglutination testing detect?
Whole-cell or insoluble antigens
What does a precipitation test require?
A gel or liquid matrix
What can immunoelectrophoresis identify?
Specific antibody classes binding antigen in serum
What does the Western blot detect?
Proteins
Who invented the original electrophoretic blotting technique, and when?
Edwin Southern, around 1975
Which four components does the complement fixation test use?
Antigen, antibody, complement and sensitized sheep red cells
What is used in fluorescent antibody testing?
A dye-labeled monoclonal antibody
What are immunoassays especially good at?
Detecting trace amounts of antigen
What distinguishes in vivo testing from serology?
Antigen is introduced directly into the body
Why do viruses present special difficulties for diagnosis?
They are not cells, and need a host cell
What kind of technique are the color-changing rapid strep tests?
A modified agglutination technique
What does phenotype mean in this context?
The physical expression of genes
What does macroscopic morphology assess?
Colony appearance on culture media
What does mannitol salts agar do?
Selects on salt, differentiates mannitol
How is a zone of inhibition interpreted?
A larger zone indicates a more effective agent
What do results of specimen analysis depend on?
Collection, handling, transport and storage
Into which two categories do results fall?
Presumptive or confirmatory
Why does faster diagnosis matter to the patient?
Proper treatment can begin in a timely manner
Who is credited with inventing the basic concept of the polymerase chain reaction?
Kary Mullis
What is G plus C content useful for?
Taxonomic determination
Why is testing for antibodies often preferred to testing for the microbe itself?
It is generally easier and more accurate
